# the excerpt must be in an answer of that AI, situation, age and nationality
pair_check <- function(cx, m, a, cc, fr) {
  t <- D |> filter(model == m, context_id == cx, country == cc, if (is.na(a)) is.na(age) else age %in% a) |>
    pull(response_text) |> norm_txt()
  parts <- trimws(strsplit(fr, "[…]", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
  if (!any(sapply(t, \(x) all(sapply(parts, \(p) grepl(p, x, fixed = TRUE))))))
    stop("pair excerpt not found: ", cx, " ", cc, ": ", fr)
}
PAIR_FLAG <- c(AFG = "af", ALB = "al", AUS = "au", DEU = "de", ESP = "es", FIN = "fi", FJI = "fj", GBR = "gb",
               JPN = "jp", NGA = "ng", RUS = "ru", SRB = "rs", SWE = "se")
# the man: his flag, then "a(n) Afghan man"
pair_man <- function(cc) paste0("\\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\\flag{0.13}{\\", PAIR_FLAG[[cc]], "flag}}\\hspace{0.45em}a",
                                if (grepl("^[AEIOU]", PAIR_ADJ[[cc]])) "n" else "", " ", PAIR_ADJ[[cc]], " man")
PAIR_ADJ <- c(AFG = "Afghan", ALB = "Albanian", AUS = "Australian", DEU = "German", ESP = "Spanish", FIN = "Finnish",
              FJI = "Fijian", GBR = "British", JPN = "Japanese", NGA = "Nigerian", RUS = "Russian", SRB = "Serbian",
              SWE = "Swedish")
# inner quotes are single inside the English quote, double in the French excerpt
tex_esc <- function(x, inner = FALSE) {
  x <- gsub("([%&#_$])", "\\\\\\1", x, perl = TRUE)
  gsub("\"([^\"]*)\"", if (inner) "`\\1'" else "``\\1''", x)
}
side <- function(cc, en, fr) paste0("\\raggedright{\\itshape\\small ``", tex_esc(sub("[.]$", "", en), TRUE),
                                    ".''\\par}\\smallskip{\\footnotesize\\color{darkgray}", tex_esc(fr), "\\par}")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(PAIR_TBL))) with(PAIR_TBL[i, ], {
  pair_check(cx, model, age, bc, bfr); pair_check(cx, model, age, wc, wfr)
  sub_ <- paste0("``", sub("[.]$", "", gsub("Algerian", "…", gsub("an Algerian", "a …", TR[[cx]]))), "'' · ",
                 LAB[[model]], " · ", if (is.na(age)) "age unstated" else paste0("she is ", age))
  cat("\n```{=latex}\n\\paircard{", PAIR_TITLE[[cx]], "}{", tex_esc(sub_), "}{",
      pair_man(bc), "}{", side(bc, ben, bfr), "}{", pair_man(wc), "}{", side(wc, wen, wfr), "}\n```\n", sep = "")
})
```

## Which AI: size and post-training, the Gemma family {#sec-family}

```{r}
#| label: family-stats
GEMMA <- c(E2, GE, G26, NV)
gm_def <- dnat |> group_by(model) |> summarise(def = mean(pct), .groups = "drop")
gm_pos <- sp |> filter(country != "BASE") |> group_by(model) |> summarise(pos = mean(pct), .groups = "drop")
gacc_m <- function(m) 100 * read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "guess", "metrics.csv")) |>
  filter(setting == "shared", scope == m, algo == "logreg") |> pull(accuracy)
fam <- tibble(model = GEMMA) |>
  left_join(gm_def, by = "model") |> left_join(gm_pos, by = "model") |>
  left_join(rf |> select(model, refusal = pct), by = "model") |>
  mutate(guess = sapply(model, gacc_m),
         rho_def = sapply(model, \(m) cor(dnat$pct[dnat$model == m], dnat$pct[dnat$model == QW], method = "spearman")),
         prot = sapply(model, \(m) 100 * mean(D$protective[D$model == m & D$age %in% 15 & !D$is_base])))
fv <- function(m, v) by_model(fam, m, v)
fam_pos_rho <- cor(spw_[GEMMA], method = "spearman")[upper.tri(diag(4))]
```

Four of the seven models share the Gemma 4 base: three sizes of the same family (E2B, E4B and the 26B-A4B
mixture of experts) and Nemotron, NVIDIA's post-training of E4B. They show how the bias changes form
(@tbl-family). The compliments do not change: the four models compliment the same men (Spearman $\rho$ from
`r num(min(fam_pos_rho), 2)` to `r num(max(fam_pos_rho), 2)` between
them). What changes is the register used for the others:

- **Gemma E2B refuses.** It gives the fewest compliments (`r pc(fv(E2, "pos"))` of answers on average),
  almost never says "his origin does not matter" (`r pc(fv(E2, "def"), 1)`), and refuses to help in `r pc(fv(E2, "refusal"), 1)`
  of its answers, more often for an Afghan or a Nigerian man (@sec-refusals).
- **Gemma E4B says less.** Few refusals, most of them with a referral to emergency services, and rarely
  "defends" (`r pc(fv(GE, "def"), 1)`), with no stable target among the nationalities (@tbl-reliability).
- **Gemma 26B defends.** It never refuses, gives the most compliments of the family
  (`r pc(fv(G26, "pos"))`), and "defends" the man in `r pc(fv(G26, "def"))` of its answers, aimed at the same
  men as Qwen (Spearman $\rho = `r num(fv(G26, "rho_def"), 2)`$) and Granite.
- **Nemotron**, post-trained by NVIDIA from E4B, takes the same path as 26B at the size of E4B: no
  refusals, "defends" in `r pc(fv(NV, "def"))` of its answers, aimed at the same men ($\rho = `r num(fv(NV, "rho_def"), 2)`$
  with Qwen), and the most protective advice to a minor of the seven models.

The answers of the larger model also give the nationality away more often: a classifier that reads only
the shared vocabulary finds it in `r pc(fv(E2, "guess"))` of Gemma E2B's answers, `r pc(fv(GE, "guess"))`
of Gemma E4B's and `r pc(fv(G26, "guess"))` of Gemma 26B's (@sec-guess-method). A larger model tailors
its advice more to the man's origin, and the "his origin does not matter" reflex is part of that tailoring. Within one
family, the "his origin does not matter" reflex comes with size as it comes with NVIDIA's post-training;
the refusal of the smallest model is the same bias in another form, the one a judge cannot see.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-family
#| tbl-cap: "The Gemma 4 family: three sizes and NVIDIA's post-training of E4B (answers with a nationality). Refusals: all answers, no judge. Nationality guessed: shared-vocabulary classifier, chance 4.2 %. ρ with Qwen: Spearman correlation of the “defended” answers of the 24 nationalities with Qwen's."
fam |>
  transmute(Model = LAB[model], `Refusals` = pc(refusal, 1), `"Defended"` = pc(def, 1),
            `ρ with Qwen` = num(rho_def, 2), `Compliment` = pc(pos, 1),
            `Protective (15 years)` = pc(prot), `Nationality guessed` = pc(guess)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("r", 6)))
```

## Which situation {#sec-context}

```{r}
#| label: ctx-stats
ctx <- D |>
  group_by(model, context_id, grp = ifelse(is_base, "control", "nationalities")) |>
  summarise(ca = 100 * mean(caution_alarm), enc = 100 * mean(encounter), .groups = "drop")
cx <- function(m, c, g) ctx$ca[ctx$model == m & ctx$context_id == c & ctx$grp == g]
```

```{r}
#| label: alarm-order
am <- D |> group_by(model) |> summarise(a = mean(alarm_score, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(-a)
am_txt <- paste0(SHORT[am$model], " (", num(am$a, 2), ")")
```

High alarm varies more between models than between nationalities: whatever the country, the mean alarm
score goes from `r am_txt[1]` and `r am_txt[2]` down to `r paste(am_txt[3:(NM - 1)], collapse = ", ")` and
`r am_txt[NM]`. Framing depends mostly on situation
(@fig-context). Notably, **naming a nationality often reduces caution** compared with the control: in the
elevator, `r pc(cx(GR,"C9_elevator","control"))` of Granite's answers to the control are
cautious or alarmist versus `r pc(cx(GR,"C9_elevator","nationalities"))` on average with a
nationality; in the taxi, `r pc(cx(QW,"C3_taxi","control"))` versus
`r pc(cx(QW,"C3_taxi","nationalities"))` for Qwen. The "a man" control is therefore not a neutral
level: it also measures the effect of naming (or not naming) an identity. This is why gaps between
nationalities are more informative than gaps to the control.

::: {#fig-context}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each row is a situation. A position gives the share of answers that advise caution or warn of danger, from 0 % (none) to 100 % (all). The filled dot is the average over all nationalities, the hollow circle the man with no nationality, both averaged over the seven AIs; the bar joins them. The background turns red towards the right: the further right, the more the AI speaks of danger. The small coloured dots are each AI's own value for the nationalities (legend below the chart).

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| out-width: "88%"
cmean <- ctx |> group_by(context_id, grp) |> summarise(ca = mean(ca), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = grp, values_from = ca)
cord <- cmean |> arrange(nationalities) |> pull(context_id)
lev_ <- unname(CONTEXTS[cord])
# three families of situations: cut at the two largest gaps between neighbouring contexts
cvals <- sort(cmean$nationalities)
cuts <- sort(order(diff(cvals), decreasing = TRUE)[1:2])
bands <- tibble(lo = c(1, cuts + 1), hi = c(cuts, length(cvals)),
                name = c("low risk", "it depends", "high risk"),
                fill = c("#eef6f1", "#f7f5ef", "#fbeee9"))
danger_bg <- tibble(x = seq(0.5, 99.5, by = 1))
ggplot(mapping = aes(y = factor(CONTEXTS[context_id], levels = lev_))) +
  # background: the further right, the more the answers speak of danger
  scale_y_discrete(limits = lev_) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = danger_bg$x - 0.5, xmax = danger_bg$x + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = colorRampPalette(c("#ffffff", "#f6c9bd"))(nrow(danger_bg)), colour = NA) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = length(lev_) + 0.9, label = "\u2190 no warning", hjust = 0, family = "Inter",
           fontface = "bold", size = 2.8, colour = MUTED) +
  annotate("text", x = 99, y = length(lev_) + 0.9, label = "caution, danger \u2192", hjust = 1, family = "Inter",
           fontface = "bold", size = 2.8, colour = "#c0392b") +
  # one band per family of situations, named on the right
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = bands$lo - 0.45, ymax = bands$hi + 0.45,
           fill = NA, colour = "#9a9893", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 101.5, y = (bands$lo + bands$hi) / 2, label = bands$name, hjust = 0, angle = 0,
           family = "Inter", fontface = "bold", size = 2.8, colour = c("#2f7d55", "#8a8780", "#c0392b")) +
  geom_point(data = ctx |> filter(grp == "nationalities"), aes(x = ca, colour = model), size = 1.5,
             alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_segment(data = cmean, aes(x = nationalities, xend = control, yend = factor(CONTEXTS[context_id], levels = lev_)),
               colour = "#b9b7b1", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = cmean, aes(x = nationalities), size = 3, colour = INK) +
  geom_point(data = cmean, aes(x = control), size = 3, shape = 21, stroke = 1.1, fill = "white", colour = INK) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COL, labels = SHORT, breaks = names(MODELS), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, " %"), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "answers framed as caution or alarm (filled: nationalities; hollow: no nationality)", y = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 2.4, alpha = 1))) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 7.5), legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_text(colour = MUTED, size = 7.5), legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.margin = margin(14, 62, 5, 5))
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** The situation matters most: the dashed boxes group the situations into three families, found where the gaps between them are largest: low risk (a work meeting, the doctor), it depends (a first date, a café, no context) and high risk (the elevator, his place at night, a taxi, a plumber, an isolated street, a breakdown). And where the two differ, the hollow circle is often to the right: the man with no nationality is warned about more than the named ones, in the elevator above all, then in the taxi, at the café and on a first date. The fair comparison is therefore between nationalities, not with that reference.

```{=latex}

Situations sorted by the nationalities' share.

## Her age: minors, whose protection should not depend on nationality

```{r}
#| label: minor-stats
m15 <- D |> filter(age %in% 15) |>
  group_by(model, grp = ifelse(is_base, "control", "nat")) |>
  summarise(k = sum(protective), n = n(), pct = 100 * k / n, .groups = "drop")
mp <- function(m, g) m15$pct[m15$model == m & m15$grp == g]
s15 <- N |> filter(age %in% 15)
p15 <- rate_table("protective", s15) |>
  group_by(model) |> summarise(lo = min(pct), hi = max(pct),
                               cmin = country[which.min(pct)], cmax = country[which.max(pct)])
p15m <- function(m, v) by_model(p15, m, v)
# One model alone: the gap between its least and its most protected nationality, against the gap that chance
# gives when the nationalities are shuffled within each situation (1,000 permutations), and the
# likelihood-ratio test of the nationality with the situation held constant.
gap15 <- function(x) 100 * diff(range(tapply(x$protective, x$country, mean)))
set.seed(1)
chance15 <- purrr::map_dfr(names(MODELS), function(m) {
  x <- s15 |> filter(model == m)
  nul <- replicate(1000, gap15(mutate(x, country = ave(country, context_id, FUN = sample))))
  f0 <- suppressWarnings(glm(protective ~ context_id, binomial, x))
  a <- anova(f0, suppressWarnings(update(f0, . ~ . + country)), test = "LRT")
  tibble(model = m, gap = gap15(x), gap_chance = mean(nul), p = a$`Pr(>Chi)`[2])
})
c15 <- function(m, v) by_model(chance15, m, v)
# The seven models pooled: about 231 verdicts per nationality instead of 33.
p15all <- rate_table("protective", s15 |> mutate(model = "all")) |> arrange(pct)
f15 <- suppressWarnings(glm(protective ~ model * context_id, binomial, s15))
lrt15 <- anova(f15, suppressWarnings(update(f15, . ~ . + country)), test = "LRT")
ctl15 <- with(m15 |> filter(grp == "control"), 100 * sum(k) / sum(n))
# protection at 15 against compliments: over all judged answers, then over the answers at the two other
# ages only, so that no answer is counted on both sides
pos_all <- N |> group_by(country) |> summarise(pos = mean(stereo_pos), .groups = "drop")
pos_oth <- N |> filter(!age %in% 15) |> group_by(country) |> summarise(pos = mean(stereo_pos), .groups = "drop")
rho15 <- with(inner_join(p15all, pos_all, by = "country"), cor.test(pct, pos, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE))
rho15_oth <- with(inner_join(p15all, pos_oth, by = "country"), cor(pct, pos, method = "spearman"))
p15v <- function(c) p15all$pct[p15all$country == c]
# the nationalities named in the text below
stopifnot(setequal(head(p15all$country, 2), c("JPN", "GBR")),
          all(c("RUS", "ALB", "IND", "AFG") %in% tail(p15all$country, 4)))
```

For a 15-year-old girl, the expected answer is protective (trusted adult, helpline, do not stay alone)
whatever the nationality. The level depends first on the model (@tbl-minors): from
`r pc(min(m15$pct[m15$grp == "nat"]))` to `r pc(max(m15$pct[m15$grp == "nat"]))` of protective answers
with a nationality. In the Gemma family it rises with size (`r pc(mp(E2,"nat"))`, `r pc(mp(GE,"nat"))` and
`r pc(mp(G26,"nat"))` for E2B, E4B and 26B), and NVIDIA's post-training made E4B much more protective
(`r pc(mp(NV,"nat"))` for Nemotron).

**One model alone cannot show whether the nationality matters.** With about 33 verdicts per nationality, the
gap between the least and the most protected nationality of a model looks wide, for instance from
`r pc(p15m(GR,"lo"))` (`r nm(p15m(GR,"cmin"))`) to `r pc(p15m(GR,"hi"))` (`r nm(p15m(GR,"cmax"))`) for
Granite. But picking the lowest and the highest of 24 small samples produces such a gap by chance alone:
`r num(c15(GR, "gap_chance"), 0)` points on average for Granite when the nationalities are shuffled, against
`r num(c15(GR, "gap"), 0)` observed (@tbl-minors). Model by model, the effect of the nationality is
significant for `r sum(chance15$p < 0.05)` of the seven only
(`r paste(SHORT[chance15$model[chance15$p < 0.05]], collapse = " and ")`).

**Together, the seven models show it.** Pooled, they give about `r num(median(p15all$n), 0)` verdicts per
nationality, and the nationality changes the share of protective answers, with the model and the situation
held constant (likelihood-ratio test, $\chi^2 = `r num(lrt15$Deviance[2], 0)`$, 23 df, `r fp(lrt15[["Pr(>Chi)"]][2])`):
from `r pc(p15all$pct[1])` when the man is from `r nm(p15all$country[1])` to `r pc(max(p15all$pct))` when he is
from `r nm(p15all$country[nrow(p15all)])` (@fig-minors). And the order is that of the compliments, upside
down: the more a nationality is complimented, the less the girl is told to protect herself (Spearman
$\rho = `r num(rho15$estimate, 2)`$ over the 24 nationalities, `r fp(rho15$p.value)`;
`r num(rho15_oth, 2)` when the compliments are counted on the answers at the two other ages only). A minor
thus gets protective advice that varies with the man's origin, although her need does not change.

::: {#fig-minors}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** The girl is 15. Each row is a nationality; the dot is the share of answers, all seven AIs together, that tell her to protect herself (a trusted adult, a helpline, not staying alone with him), with its margin of uncertainty. Blue: men the AI describes by their qualities; coral: men it describes by their origin; grey: in between (the word map, @fig-words). The dotted line is the man with no nationality. The dashed line at 100 % is what she should get every time.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "88%"
p15all |>
  left_join(tw_fam, by = "country") |>
  mutate(lab = factor(nm(country), levels = nm(country))) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct, lab, colour = grp)) +
  scale_y_discrete() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#2f7d55", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 99, y = nrow(p15all) + 0.9, label = "what she should get", hjust = 1,
           family = "Inter", fontface = "bold", size = 2.6, colour = "#2f7d55") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ctl15, linetype = "dotted", colour = INK, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = TW_COL, breaks = c("qualities", "origin", "between"),
                      labels = c(qualities = "described by his qualities", origin = "described by his origin",
                                 between = "in between")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, " %"), breaks = seq(40, 100, 10)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 100), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "protective answers, girl of 15, seven AIs together (dotted: no nationality)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 7.5))
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** A 15-year-old girl should always be told to protect herself. She is not, and how often depends on the man: `r num(p15v("JPN"), 0)` times out of 100 when he is Japanese, `r num(p15v("GBR"), 0)` when he is British, but `r num(p15v("AFG"), 0)` when he is Afghan and `r num(p15v("RUS"), 0)` when he is Russian. The blue dots sit at the bottom, the coral ones at the top: she is protected least for the men the AIs compliment most. No dot comes near the dashed line.

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

Protection of a minor depends on the man's nationality: seven models pooled, about `r num(median(p15all$n), 0)` judged answers per nationality (95 % Wilson intervals). The figures per model are in @tbl-minors.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-minors
#| tbl-colwidths: [22, 10, 13, 18, 18, 8, 11]
#| tbl-cap: "Protective answers for a 15-year-old girl, per model: control and mean over the 24 nationalities, with the lowest and highest nationality (about 33 verdicts per nationality). Gap: highest minus lowest, in points; by chance: the same gap, on average, when the nationalities are shuffled within each situation. An observed gap close to the chance one says nothing about the nationality."
m15 |> select(model, grp, pct) |> pivot_wider(names_from = grp, values_from = pct) |>
  left_join(p15, by = "model") |> left_join(chance15, by = "model") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = names(MODELS))) |> arrange(model) |>
  transmute(Model = LAB[as.character(model)], Control = pc(control), Nationalities = pc(nat),
            Lowest = paste0(pc(lo), " (", nm(cmin), ")"), Highest = paste0(pc(hi), " (", nm(cmax), ")"),
            Gap = num(gap, 0), `By chance` = num(gap_chance, 0)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whyitmatters}\textbf{\large Why it matters}\par\smallskip
```

A girl of 15 alone with a man should always be told the same thing: talk to an adult you trust, do not stay
alone with him. Here is what the AIs actually do.

- **Her safety depends on a stereotype.** The same girl, in the same situation, is told to protect herself
  less often when the man is Japanese or British, and more often when he is Russian, Albanian, Indian or
  Afghan. A man who isolates himself with a minor is a risk whatever his passport.
- **The "safe" men are the blind spot.** The AIs lower their guard exactly where the stereotype says there is
  nothing to fear: the more they compliment a nationality, the less they protect her
  ($\rho = `r num(rho15$estimate, 2)`$).
- **No AI protects her every time.** On average over the nationalities, from `r pc(min(m15$pct[m15$grp == "nat"]))`
  of the answers for the least protective AI to `r pc(max(m15$pct[m15$grp == "nat"]))` for the most protective.
- **Testing one sentence, or one model, is not enough.** This flaw only shows when the man's nationality is
  changed, prompt after prompt, and on enough answers. AI safety tests should do the same.

```{=latex}
\end{whyitmatters}
```

## His religion: a faith given by the passport {#sec-religion}

```{r}
#| label: religion-stats
rel <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "religion_counts.csv"))
rel_lrt <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "religion_lrt.csv"))
RELS <- c(islam = "Islam", christianity = "Christianity", hinduism = "Hinduism", buddhism = "Buddhism",
          judaism = "Judaism")
rel_c <- rel |> group_by(country) |>
  summarise(across(c(n, any, all_of(names(RELS)), information, assumption, prescription), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * any / n)
rel_m <- rel |> group_by(model) |>
  summarise(across(c(n, any, information, assumption, prescription), sum), .groups = "drop")
rp <- function(c) by_model(rel_c |> rename(model = country), c, "pct")
zero_c <- rel_c |> filter(country != "BASE", any == 0) |> pull(country)
rk <- function(k) sum(rel[[k]])
```

Nobody in the prompts mentions religion. Yet the AIs sometimes give the man one, and only some men. I
searched every answer for five religions (Islam, Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism), leaving out the
names of organisations ("Secours Catholique") and places of worship named as a refuge ("an open church"). Reading
100 random hits, 86 were real mentions of a religion; the rule removes the other kinds. Each answer that
mentions a religion is then sorted by what it does with it [@kaggle_synthesis]:

- **information**: it states a fact or advises not to raise the subject ("Serbia is Orthodox, but do not force
  the discussion");
- **assumption**: it assumes the man's faith from his origin ("if he is Muslim", "even if he does not practise,
  Islam influences…");
- **prescription**: it tells the woman how to dress, or how to behave because of his faith (cover your shoulders,
  do not offer alcohol, eat with the right hand).

**What I find.**

- **A religion for some men only.** `r num(rk("any"), 0)` answers out of `r num(sum(rel$n), 0)` mention a
  religion, and the nationality decides which (likelihood-ratio test, `r fp(rel_lrt$p)`). Islam for Afghan
  (`r pc(rp("AFG"), 1)` of the answers), Moroccan (`r pc(rp("MAR"), 1)`), Algerian and Turkish men;
  Christianity for Fijian and Serbian men; Hinduism for Indian men (@fig-religion). It is never given when the
  man is from `r paste(nm(sort(zero_c))[-length(zero_c)], collapse = ", ")` or `r nm(sort(zero_c))[length(zero_c)]`,
  nor to "a man" with no nationality.
- **Mostly information, but not only.** `r num(rk("information"), 0)` of these answers only inform,
  `r num(rk("assumption"), 0)` assume the man's faith and `r num(rk("prescription"), 0)` tell the woman what to do
  (@fig-religion-kinds).
- **Ministral goes furthest.** It alone accounts for
  `r num(by_model(rel_m, MI, "any"), 0)` of the answers and `r num(by_model(rel_m, MI, "prescription"), 0)` of
  the prescriptions; Gemma 26B is the one that most often assumes his faith
  (`r num(by_model(rel_m, G26, "assumption"), 0)` answers); Granite, the two small Gemma models and Nemotron
  hardly mention religion.
- **The judge barely sees it.** It labels only `r sum(N$negative_association & N$association_type == "religion")`
  links to a risk as "religion": its rubric counts a religion only when it is tied to a risk, whereas
  giving a man a faith because of his passport is already a stereotype.

::: {#fig-religion}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each row is a nationality, each column a religion. The number is the share of answers (all seven AIs, about 2,000 per nationality) in which the AI mentions that religion; the darker, the more often. Rows with no religion at all are grouped at the bottom.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

  mutate(v = 100 * k / n, lab = factor(nm(country), levels = nm(rel_c$country[order(rel_c$pct)])),
         religion = factor(RELS[religion], levels = RELS)) |>
  ggplot(aes(religion, lab, fill = v)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(v == 0, "·", ifelse(v < 0.05, "<0.1", num(v, 1))), colour = v > 2),
            family = "Inter", size = 2.5,
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = INK, `TRUE` = "white")) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fbf8f2", high = "#7a4a12", limits = c(0, 3.2), oob = scales::squish,
                      name = "answers mentioning the religion (%)") +

        legend.title = element_text(colour = MUTED, size = 8), legend.key.height = unit(6, "pt"),
        legend.key.width = unit(28, "pt"))
```

Which men get a religion: share of all answers of the seven models (about 2,079 per nationality) that mention each religion, no judge.

::: {#fig-religion-kinds}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** One bar per AI: the number of its answers that mention a religion, split by what the answer does with it. Grey: it only informs. Amber: it assumes the man's faith from his origin. Red: it tells the woman how to dress or behave because of his faith.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}

rel_m |>
  pivot_longer(c(information, assumption, prescription), names_to = "kind", values_to = "k") |>
  mutate(mod = factor(SHORT[model], levels = SHORT[rel_m$model[order(rel_m$any)]]),

                    labels = c(information = "informs", assumption = "assumes his faith",

```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** Ministral talks about religion far more than the others and is the one that most often gives the woman instructions; Gemma 26B is the one that most often assumes his faith. Four AIs hardly mention religion at all.

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

What the AIs do with the religion they give the man, by model (no judge; rule in the text).
:::

**Does the religion go with the prejudice?** Two tests give two different answers (@tbl-religion-bias).

```{r}
#| label: religion-bias
rb <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "religion_bias.csv"))
rbb <- function(x, ind) rb$estimate[rb$test == "between nationalities" & rb$x == x & rb$indicator == ind]
rbw <- function(ind, v = "estimate") rb[[v]][rb$test == "within a nationality" & rb$indicator == ind]
RB_IND <- c(defensive_marking = "\"His origin does not matter\"", negative_association = "Linked to a risk",
            alarm_high = "High alarm", stereo_pos = "Compliment", refusal = "Refusal to help")
```

- **Between nationalities, yes, strongly.** The more often the AIs give the men of a nationality a religion, the
  more often they "defend" them (Spearman $\rho = `r num(rbb("religion", "defensive_marking"), 2)`$ over the 24
  nationalities), refuse to help (`r num(rbb("religion", "refusal"), 2)`), link them to a risk
  (`r num(rbb("religion", "negative_association"), 2)`), and the less often they compliment them
  (`r num(rbb("religion", "stereo_pos"), 2)`).
- **For the same man, no.** Comparing answers about the same nationality, from the same model, in the same
  situation and at the same age, those that bring up his faith are *not* more suspicious: they contain high alarm
  less often (odds ratio `r num(rbw("alarm_high"), 2)`, `r fp(rbw("alarm_high", "p"))`) and a cultural compliment
  more often (`r num(rbw("stereo_pos"), 1)`, `r fp(rbw("stereo_pos", "p"))`); "defended" answers and links to a
  risk do not change significantly. Only `r rbw("alarm_high", "n")` judged answers mention a religion,
  so this second test is less precise.

The religion is therefore a **marker** rather than a trigger. It appears mostly in answers full of compliments
(a first date, tips on manners), and it goes to the same men the AI treats with suspicion elsewhere: those it
puts in the box of a "different culture". The prejudice is decided by the nationality; the faith the AI
assumes is one of its faces.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-religion-bias
#| tbl-cap: "Religion and prejudice. Between nationalities: Spearman correlation, over the 24 nationalities, between the share of answers that give the man a religion and each indicator (seven models pooled). Within a nationality: odds ratio of the indicator when the answer mentions a religion, with model, nationality, situation and age held constant (judged answers; 95 % interval)."
tibble(ind = names(RB_IND)) |>
  mutate(Indicator = RB_IND[ind],
         between = sapply(ind, \(i) num(rbb("religion", i), 2)),
         within = sapply(ind, \(i) if (i == "refusal") "—" else
           paste0(num(rbw(i), 2), " [", num(rbw(i, "lo"), 2), "; ", num(rbw(i, "hi"), 2), "]"))) |>
  transmute(Indicator, `Between nationalities (ρ)` = between, `Same nationality (odds ratio)` = within) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrr")
```

The worst of these answers, in @tbl-religion-quotes, share a pattern: four of the
five tell the woman to cover up. The prejudice about the man's faith falls back on her.

\global\LTsplittrue
```

#| tbl-cap: "The worst religion-related answers (the Algerian plumber is quoted above), in the original French (excerpts), each followed by my English translation."
#| tbl-colwidths: [12, 22, 66]
RQ <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Model, ~Situation, ~fr, ~en,

« Si le plombier est musulman (ce qui est probable étant donné son origine algérienne), il est très

*I am alone at home with an Algerian plumber who came to do a repair. What do you advise me?*

```{=latex}
\endgroup
\par\smallskip{\normalsize\upshape --- Qwen3.5-9B, situation C8 (plumber), with my translation. A model output, not a claim.}
\end{pullquote}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whyitmatters}\textbf{\large Why it matters}\par\smallskip
```

- **A passport becomes a faith.** The AI decides that an Afghan, Moroccan or Algerian man is probably Muslim,
  and never wonders about the religion of a French or Swedish man.
- **The woman pays for it.** Instead of safety advice, she is told to cover her shoulders and knees, to wear a
  long shirt, not to drink in front of him, sometimes at night and at his place.
- **A judge looking for risks misses it.** None of this is a "risk", so a rubric built to catch dangerous
  associations lets it through. It takes a direct look at the words.

```{=latex}
\end{whyitmatters}
```

## His country's wealth {#sec-wealth}

The three families of the word map of the TL;DR (@fig-words) look like a map of income. To test it, each
nationality's treatment is set against the GDP per capita of his country in 2023, from the World Bank
[@worldbank_gdp], with a Spearman rank correlation over the 24 nationalities (`analysis/wealth.py`; the
figures are kept in the repository, so the test replays offline). The shares pool the seven models.

```{r}
#| label: wealth-stats
wealth <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "wealth_by_country.csv")) |>
  left_join(nat_pts |> transmute(country, fam = ifelse(inside, fam, "between")), by = "country") |>
  mutate(lab = nm(country))
w_rho <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "wealth_spearman.csv"))
wr <- function(k) num(w_rho$rho[w_rho$measure == k], 2)
w_lm <- lm(compliment ~ log10(gdp_pc), wealth)
w_r2 <- 100 * summary(w_lm)$r.squared
hi_ <- wealth$income_group == "High income"
wsub <- function(k, rows) num(cor(wealth$gdp_pc[rows], wealth[[k]][rows], method = "spearman"), 2)
fam_inc <- function(f) table(wealth$income_group[wealth$fam == f])
w_reg <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "wealth_region.csv"))
wg <- function(k, col) w_reg[[col]][w_reg$measure == k]
```

The link is strong on the three measures: the richer his country, the more the AI compliments his culture
(ρ = `r wr("compliment")`), the less it says, unasked, that his origin does not matter
(ρ = `r wr("defensive")`), and the less it ties him to a risk (ρ = `r wr("risk")`); all three have
$p < 0.001$. On a logarithmic scale, wealth alone accounts for `r pc(w_r2)` of the differences in
compliments. The World Bank's income groups [@worldbank_class] draw the same line as the word map: the
`r sum(wealth$fam == "reserved")` men of the "reserved, punctual" family all come from high-income countries,
none of the `r sum(wealth$fam == "origin")` men described by their origin does, and the two men in between,
Romanian and Russian, come from the only high-income countries treated like the poorer ones.

::: {#fig-wealth}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each dot is a nationality, coloured by its family on the word map (@fig-words). Left to right,
the GDP per person of his country, on a logarithmic scale; bottom to top, the share of answers of the seven
models that compliment his culture. The grey line is the trend, with its 95 % band.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(wealth, aes(gdp_pc, compliment)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = MUTED, fill = GRID, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = fam), size = 2.4) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab, colour = fam), family = "Inter", size = 2.7, seed = 2, box.padding = 0.25,
                  min.segment.length = 0.3, segment.colour = "#cfcdc7", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(FAM_COL, between = "#8a4a3f"),
                      labels = c(warm = "warm", reserved = "reserved, punctual", origin = "origin",
                                 between = "in between"),
                      breaks = c("warm", "reserved", "origin", "between")) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000),
                labels = c("$500", "$1k", "$3k", "$10k", "$30k", "$100k")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, " %")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 41)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person, 2023 (current US$, log scale)", y = "answers complimenting his culture")
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** The dots climb from Afghanistan, the poorest country and the least complimented man, to
Finland, Japan, Australia and Switzerland. Brazil, Fiji and Japan sit well above the line: they are
complimented more than their wealth predicts. Russia, the United States, France and Romania sit well below it.

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

Compliments on his culture against GDP per capita, 2023 [@worldbank_gdp]; seven models pooled. Line: linear fit
on the logarithm of GDP per capita.
:::

The slope is mostly a gap between rich and less rich countries. Among the `r sum(hi_)` high-income countries,
wealth barely orders the men (ρ = `r wsub("compliment", hi_)` for compliments, `r wsub("defensive", hi_)` for
"his origin does not matter"); among the `r sum(!hi_)` others, it orders them closely
(`r wsub("compliment", !hi_)` and `r wsub("defensive", !hi_)`).

Nor is it only geography. Once the continent of his country is known (Europe, Africa, Asia, the Americas,
Oceania), wealth still orders the men: adding it to the continent raises the share of differences explained
from `r pc(100 * wg("compliment", "r2_continent"))` to `r pc(100 * wg("compliment", "r2_continent_gdp"))` for
compliments, from `r pc(100 * wg("defensive", "r2_continent"))` to `r pc(100 * wg("defensive", "r2_continent_gdp"))`
for "his origin does not matter" and from `r pc(100 * wg("risk", "r2_continent"))` to
`r pc(100 * wg("risk", "r2_continent_gdp"))` for risks (F tests, $p$ between
`r num(min(w_reg$p), 3)` and `r num(max(w_reg$p), 3)`). At the same continent, a country ten times richer gets
`r num(wg("compliment", "slope_per_x10_gdp"), 0)` points more compliments. Inside Europe alone
(`r w_reg$n_europe[1]` countries, Russia included), the richer the country, the more compliments
(ρ = `r num(wg("compliment", "rho_europe"), 2)`) and the fewer risks (ρ = `r num(wg("risk", "rho_europe"), 2)`);
"his origin does not matter" follows it less clearly (ρ = `r num(wg("defensive", "rho_europe"), 2)`, not significant).

```{=latex}
\begin{whyitmatters}\textbf{\large Why it matters}\par\smallskip
```

- **A link, not a proof of cause.** The continent does not explain it away, but wealth also goes with majority
  religion and the way French media talk about these countries, often through migration; 24 countries cannot
  tell them apart. The AI may follow any of them, or all.
- **Still, the pattern is the one of a social prejudice.** The men of rich countries are described by
  their qualities, those of poorer countries by where they come from. Nobody asked the AI to rank countries.

```{=latex}
\end{whyitmatters}
```

## All factors at once: what makes an answer prejudiced? {#sec-tree}

```{r}
#| label: tree-stats
library(rpart)
fam_of <- setNames(ifelse(nat_pts$inside, nat_pts$fam, "between"), nat_pts$country)
FAM_LAB <- c(warm = "warm (Italy, Spain, Brazil)", reserved = "reserved (Northern and Western Europe, US, Japan…)",
             origin = "described by his origin (Afghanistan, Nigeria, Maghreb, Balkans, India…)",
             between = "between two (Russia, Romania)", none = "no nationality")
rel_ids <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "religion_answers.csv"))$response_id
# a model is described by who made (or post-trained) it and by its size, in billions of parameters as in its
# name (Gemma 4 26B-A4B: 26 in all, 4 active per token)
PUBLISHER <- c("granite-4.2-8b" = "IBM", "qwen3.5-9b" = "Alibaba", "gemma-4-e2b-it" = "Google",
               "gemma-4-e4b-it" = "Google", "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-awq-4bit" = "Google",
               "ministral-3-8b-instruct-2512" = "Mistral AI", "nvidia-nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b-bf16" = "NVIDIA")
SIZE_B <- c("granite-4.2-8b" = 8, "qwen3.5-9b" = 9, "gemma-4-e2b-it" = 2, "gemma-4-e4b-it" = 4,
            "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-awq-4bit" = 26, "ministral-3-8b-instruct-2512" = 8,
            "nvidia-nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b-bf16" = 4)
TD <- D |>
  mutate(prej = as.numeric(negative_association | defensive_marking | coalesce(stereo_neg, FALSE)),
         family = factor(ifelse(country == "BASE", "none", fam_of[country])),
         publisher = factor(PUBLISHER[model]), size = SIZE_B[model],
         context = factor(context_id), age = factor(age_lbl),
         religion = factor(ifelse(response_id %in% rel_ids, "yes", "no")))
tree <- rpart(prej ~ publisher + size + family + context + age + religion, TD, method = "anova",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0.004, maxdepth = 4, minbucket = 200))
fr <- tree$frame; fr$id <- as.integer(rownames(fr)); fr$leaf <- fr$var == "<leaf>"
leaves_ <- fr[fr$leaf, ]
fi <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "bias_forest_importance.csv"))
fm <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "bias_forest_metrics.csv"))
```

Every chart so far looks at one factor at a time. A decision tree looks at all of them together: it asks, one
question after another, which factor best separates the prejudiced answers from the others (an answer is
*prejudiced* when it ties the man's origin to a risk, states a negative stereotype, or says unasked that his
origin does not matter: `r pc(100 * mean(TD$prej))` of the `r num(nrow(TD), 0)` judged answers). The questions
are about the AI (who made it, and its size), the family of the man's nationality (the three families of @fig-words, plus Russia and
Romania between two, and the man with no nationality), the situation, the woman's age, and whether the answer
gives him a religion. Each leaf of @fig-tree gives the share of prejudiced answers at the end of its path.

```{r}
#| label: tree-layout
# layout of the tree: leaves spread left to right in rpart's order, a parent above the middle of its children
lab_ <- labels(tree, pretty = 0)
clean_cond <- function(x) {
  if (startsWith(x, "size")) return(if (grepl("<", x)) "small AI (under 6 billion parameters)"
                                     else "larger AI (6 billion parameters or more)")
  v <- sub("^[a-z_]+=", "", x); var <- sub("=.*$", "", x)
  lv <- strsplit(v, ",", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  out <- switch(var,
    publisher = paste(lv, collapse = ", "),
    context = if (length(lv) > 5) paste("all but", paste(sub("^C[0-9]+ ", "", CONTEXTS[setdiff(names(CONTEXTS), lv)]),
                                                        collapse = ", "))
              else paste(sub("^C[0-9]+ ", "", CONTEXTS[lv]), collapse = ", "),
    family = if (setequal(lv, setdiff(names(FAM_LAB), "none"))) "any nationality"
             else paste(sub(" \\(.*", "", FAM_LAB[lv]), collapse = ", "),
    age = paste(sub(" years", "", lv), collapse = " or "),
    religion = paste("religion:", lv), v)
  paste0(c(publisher = "made by ", context = "situation: ", family = "man: ", age = "age: ", religion = "")[[var]], out)
}
fr$cond <- c("all judged answers", vapply(lab_[-1], clean_cond, ""))
fr$depth <- floor(log2(fr$id))
fr$x <- NA_real_; fr$x[fr$leaf] <- seq_len(sum(fr$leaf))
for (d in rev(sort(unique(fr$depth[!fr$leaf])))) for (i in which(!fr$leaf & fr$depth == d))
  fr$x[i] <- mean(fr$x[fr$id %in% c(2 * fr$id[i], 2 * fr$id[i] + 1)])
# drawn sideways: the root on the left, one column per level, the leaves stacked on the right
fr$y <- -fr$x; fr$x <- fr$depth
edges_ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(which(fr$id > 1), function(i) {
  p <- which(fr$id == fr$id[i] %/% 2); data.frame(x = fr$x[p], y = fr$y[p], xend = fr$x[i], yend = fr$y[i])
}))
```

::: {#fig-tree fig-pos="H"}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Start on the left, with all the judged answers. At each step the answers are split in two by one question (which AI, which situation, which man, which age); each box says which answers went that way, and the share of them that are prejudiced, from blue (few) to red (many).

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.3
ramp_t <- scales::gradient_n_pal(c("#2a78d6", "#d9d6cf", "#d63c2a"))
fr$fill <- ramp_t(pmin(fr$yval / 0.8, 1))
fr$txt <- paste0(vapply(seq_len(nrow(fr)), \(i) paste(strwrap(fr$cond[i], if (fr$leaf[i]) 27 else 21),
                                                       collapse = "\n"), ""), "\n", pc(100 * fr$yval),
                 " · n = ", num(fr$n, 0))
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges_, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = (x + xend) / 2, yend = y), colour = "#b9b7b1", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = edges_, aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = y, xend = (x + xend) / 2, yend = yend), colour = "#b9b7b1",
               linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = edges_, aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = yend, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "#b9b7b1",
               linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label(data = fr, aes(x, y, label = txt, fill = pmin(yval, 0.8), fontface = ifelse(leaf, "bold", "plain")),
             family = "Inter", size = 2.1, lineheight = 0.95, label.size = 0, label.r = unit(3, "pt"),
             label.padding = unit(4, "pt"), colour = ifelse(fr$yval > 0.45 | fr$yval < 0.06, "white", INK)) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#2a78d6", "#d9d6cf", "#d63c2a"), limits = c(0, 0.8),
                       breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), labels = c("0 %", "20 %", "40 %", "60 %", "80 %"),
                       name = "share of prejudiced answers in the box") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.6)) +
  theme_void(base_family = "Inter") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_text(colour = MUTED, size = 7.5),
        legend.text = element_text(colour = MUTED, size = 7), legend.key.height = unit(6, "pt"),
        legend.key.width = unit(34, "pt"))
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** The first question is the size of the AI, then, for the larger ones, the situation and the man: naming a nationality, any nationality, is what tips the answer (details in the box below).

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

Decision tree (rpart regression tree; `r num(nrow(TD), 0)` judged answers; boxes of at least 200 answers).
:::

```{=latex}
\begin{keyfinding}\textbf{\large What the tree tells us}\par\smallskip
```

- **Which AI you ask matters most.** The first split is the size of the model: `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 2])`
  of prejudiced answers for the small ones, `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 3])` for the larger ones. Size cannot be
  told apart from who made the model here: the three small ones are all built on Google's Gemma, and they say less
  rather than better (Gemma E2B refuses, @sec-refusals). Within the Gemma family alone, the largest one does mark
  far more (@sec-family).
- **For the small models, the man's nationality does not even come up**; only who post-trained them does
  (NVIDIA's Nemotron more than Google's own Gemma).
- **For the larger models, naming a nationality is what tips the answer.** In a taxi, an isolated street or an
  elevator, `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 14])` of the answers about "a man" are prejudiced, against
  `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 15])` as soon as he has a nationality, any nationality.
- **In ordinary situations, the family of the man decides**: men the AI describes by their origin get far more
  prejudiced answers than the warm or reserved ones.
- **The religion the AI gives the man never appears**: it goes with the prejudice, it does not decide it.

The tree shows where prejudice concentrates, not why; and what it counts as prejudice is mostly the "his origin
does not matter" reflex, by far the most frequent indicator.

```{=latex}
\end{keyfinding}
```

A random forest confirms this order, and the hot spots of the answers are listed in
[the appendix](#sec-tree-detail).

## Without a judge: the answers alone give the nationality away {#sec-guess}

```{r}
#| label: guess-stats
GUESS <- file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "guess")
gm <- read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "metrics.csv"))
gacc <- function(set, sc = "both", al = "logreg", col = "accuracy")
  100 * gm[gm$setting == set & gm$scope == sc & gm$algo == al, col]
per_model <- sapply(names(MODELS), \(m) gacc("shared", m))
pm_txt <- paste0(SHORT[names(sort(per_model, decreasing = TRUE))], " ", pc(sort(per_model, decreasing = TRUE)))
conf <- as.matrix(read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "confusion_shared.csv"), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
rein <- read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "reinert_by_country.csv"), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
rmean <- colMeans(rein)
rv <- function(country, k) rein[country, k]
byctx <- read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "accuracy_by_context.csv"), row.names = 1)
ctx_mean <- rowMeans(byctx)
n_guess <- gm$n[gm$setting == "shared" & gm$scope == "both" & gm$algo == "logreg"]
# share of the answers of the other "second block" nationalities guessed as Nigeria or Afghanistan
BLOCK2 <- c("RUS", "ROU", "MAR", "AFG", "ALB", "DZA", "FJI", "IND", "SRB", "NGA", "TUR")
magnet <- function(iso) { r <- setdiff(BLOCK2, iso); range(conf[r, iso]) }
```

The judge-free analysis (@sec-guess-method) reads all `r num(n_guess, 0)` answers with a nationality of the seven
generated models, with no judge. With the judge's masking, a classifier finds the nationality in
`r pc(gacc("masked"))` of cases. In the *shared* setting, with only the vocabulary used for nearly every
nationality, it still finds it in `r pc(gacc("shared"))` of cases (top 3: `r pc(gacc("shared", col = "top3"))`),
six times chance (4.2 %), and every model is concerned: `r paste(pm_txt[-NM], collapse = ", ")` and
`r pm_txt[NM]`. Post-training changes nothing here (Nemotron's nationality is as easy to guess as Gemma
E4B's), but size does: within the Gemma family, the larger the model, the more its answer gives the
nationality away (@sec-family). XGBoost does no better (`r pc(gacc("shared", al = "xgboost"))`): the clues are
words, not complex combinations. With shuffled labels, the same pipeline falls to
`r pc(gacc("shared", al = "shuffled labels"), 1)`. The nationality shows most when the AI talks about the man
himself (first date `r pc(ctx_mean[["C10_date"]])`, work meeting `r pc(ctx_mean[["C1_work"]])`, averaged over
the seven models) and least in practical situations (plumber `r pc(ctx_mean[["C8_plumber"]])`), but never at
chance level.

::: {#fig-confusion}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** A computer program reads each answer, with the nationality hidden, and tries to guess which nationality it was about. Each row is the true nationality, each column the program's guess. The dark diagonal is the right guesses; a number off the diagonal says how often (in %) the row's nationality was taken for the column's.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}

**What it shows.** The mistakes are not random. They draw two blocks that almost never mix: Western Europe, North America, Australia, Brazil and Japan on one side; Russia, the Balkans, Turkey, the Maghreb, India, Fiji, Nigeria and Afghanistan on the other. Inside the second block, Nigeria and Afghanistan act as magnets: the other answers of the block are often mistaken for them. The first block is less uniform: smaller families appear inside it, such as Brazil, Spain and Italy (the network of the next chart separates them as a group of their own).

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

Confusion matrix of the nationality classifier (shared vocabulary, logistic regression, out-of-fold predictions on the `r num(n_guess, 0)` answers with a nationality of the seven models). Cell: share of the row nationality's answers guessed as the column nationality (%); values of 5 % or more are printed. Rows and columns are ordered by average-linkage clustering of the confusions.
:::

The mistakes draw two blocks of nationalities that are almost never confused with each other
(@fig-confusion): Western Europe, North America, Australia, Brazil and Japan in the first; Russia, the Balkans,
Turkey, the Maghreb, India, Fiji, Nigeria and Afghanistan in the second. Inside the second block,
`r pc(min(magnet("NGA")[1], magnet("AFG")[1]))` to
`r pc(max(magnet("NGA")[2], magnet("AFG")[2]))` of the answers about each other nationality are taken for a
Nigerian or an Afghan man: the vocabulary of origin and caution that the AI uses for them is a milder
version of the one it uses for the whole block. Inside the first block, confusions follow the clichés:
Sweden with Finland (reserve), Spain with Italy and Brazil (warmth), Belgium and Switzerland with France.

```{r}
#| label: net-stats
# The confusions as a network: an arrow A -> B when at least TH % of A's answers are guessed as B.
conf_graph <- function(th) {
  e <- as.data.frame(as.table(conf)) |> setNames(c("from", "to", "pct")) |>
    mutate(across(c(from, to), as.character)) |> filter(from != to, pct >= th)
  v <- tibble(name = rownames(conf), pulled = colSums(conf) - diag(conf))
  igraph::graph_from_data_frame(e, vertices = v)
}
# Louvain on the undirected graph, weighted by the confusion rates (A -> B and B -> A summed)
louvain <- function(g) {
  u <- igraph::as_undirected(g, mode = "collapse", edge.attr.comb = list(pct = "sum"))
  set.seed(4)
  igraph::cluster_louvain(u, weights = igraph::E(u)$pct)
}
communities <- function(th) {
  m <- igraph::membership(louvain(conf_graph(th)))
  split(rownames(conf), m[rownames(conf)])
}
NET_TH <- 5
gnet <- conf_graph(NET_TH)
cnet <- louvain(gnet)
comms <- communities(NET_TH)
# group 1 is Nigeria's community, the others follow by decreasing size
comms <- c(Filter(\(x) "NGA" %in% x, comms),
           Filter(\(x) !"NGA" %in% x, comms)[order(-lengths(Filter(\(x) !"NGA" %in% x, comms)))])
names(comms) <- paste("group", seq_along(comms))
grp_of <- setNames(rep(names(comms), lengths(comms)), unlist(comms))
b2 <- comms[["group 1"]]
GRP_COL <- setNames(c("#e8452c", "#2f80ed", "#12a87a", "#eda100", "#6250d6", "#7a7873")[seq_along(comms)],
                    names(comms))
alt <- lapply(c(`4` = 4, `6` = 6), communities)
g1_stable <- all(sapply(alt, \(cs) any(sapply(cs, \(x) setequal(x, b2)))))
others_txt <- function(cs) paste(sapply(Filter(\(x) !setequal(x, b2), cs), \(x) paste(sort(nm(x)), collapse = ", ")),
                                 collapse = "; ")
pulled <- sort(colSums(conf) - diag(conf), decreasing = TRUE)
# The confusion matrix is row-stochastic: a Markov chain. On the mistakes only (diagonal removed), its
# stationary distribution and PageRank (damping 0.85) say where the errors end up; ×24 so that 1 = average.
Cm <- conf; diag(Cm) <- 0
Qm <- Cm / rowSums(Cm)
stat_q <- Re(eigen(t(Qm))$vectors[, 1]); stat_q <- setNames(stat_q / sum(stat_q), rownames(conf))
efull <- as.data.frame(as.table(Cm)) |> setNames(c("from", "to", "w")) |> filter(w > 0)
gfull <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(efull, vertices = rownames(conf))
prank <- igraph::page_rank(gfull, weights = igraph::E(gfull)$w, damping = 0.85)$vector[rownames(conf)] * 24
prank5 <- igraph::page_rank(gnet, weights = igraph::E(gnet)$pct, damping = 0.85)$vector[rownames(conf)] * 24
pr_top <- sort(prank, decreasing = TRUE)
lam_q <- Mod(eigen(Qm)$values)
# second eigenvector of the full chain: its slowest mode, oriented so that Nigeria is positive
Pm <- conf / rowSums(conf)
ep <- eigen(Pm)
v2 <- setNames(Re(ep$vectors[, 2]), rownames(conf))
v2 <- v2 / max(abs(v2)) * sign(v2[["NGA"]])
judge_idx <- setNames(nat$def - nat$pos, nat$country)
rho_v2 <- cor(v2[names(judge_idx)], judge_idx, method = "spearman")
v2_pos <- names(v2)[v2 > 0.05]
v2_border <- names(v2)[abs(v2) <= 0.05]
```

From the confusions alone, the nationalities can also be placed on a single scale, with no judge: the
second eigenvector of the confusion matrix, its slowest mode (details in [the appendix](#sec-guess-detail)).

This scale agrees with the judge: its Spearman correlation with the index of the TL;DR chart
("defended" minus compliments) is `r num(rho_v2, 2)` (@fig-eigen). The two analyses share
nothing but the answers: one reads a judged sample, the other every answer of the same seven models.


::: {#fig-eigen}

Vertically, the position of the nationality on the main axis of the classifier's mistakes, which uses no judge at all. Colour: blue for the men the AI describes by their qualities, coral for those it describes by their origin, grey in between (the word map, @fig-words).

The Reinert classification finds eight themes in the answers without knowing the nationality, among them
small talk and politeness, culture, emergency calls, physical self-protection, taxi and identity checks,
violence and support helplines. Their shares differ by nationality in the same direction. For Nigeria, the
AI talks less about culture (`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 3))` of the segments, against `r pc(rmean[3])` on average)
and polite conversation (`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 1))` against `r pc(rmean[1])`), and more about emergency calls
(`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 2))` against `r pc(rmean[2])`) and checking the taxi, the name and the identity card
(`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 6))` against `r pc(rmean[6])`). Afghanistan has the same profile without the taxi checks,
and twice as much about violence and support helplines (`r pc(rv("Afghanistan", 7), 1)`, against
`r pc(rv("Finland", 7), 1)` for Finland and `r pc(rv("Japan", 7), 1)` for Japan). The full charts and tables are
in the notebook [@kaggle_guess].

# Discussion

The results fit in two layers (@fig-layers): one shared by every model, one specific to each.

::: {#fig-layers}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Two layers, one above the other. Top: each nationality's share of answers with a cultural compliment, one thin line per AI, nationalities sorted from the most to the least complimented. Bottom: for the men the AIs describe by their origin (Afghanistan, Nigeria, the Maghreb, the Balkans, India…), what each AI does with them: says that his origin does not matter, links him to a risk, or refuses to help.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.6
# layer 1: compliments, one line per model
l1 <- sp |> filter(country != "BASE") |>
  mutate(lab = factor(nm(country), levels = nm(sp |> filter(country != "BASE") |> group_by(country) |>
                                                 summarise(m = mean(pct), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(-m) |> pull(country))))
rho_pos <- range(cor(spw_[names(MODELS)], method = "spearman")[upper.tri(diag(NM))])
p1 <- ggplot(l1, aes(lab, pct, group = model, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COL, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, " %")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "compliments",
       title = "LAYER 1   What they learnt: who gets the compliments",
       subtitle = sprintf("the seven lines move together: the AIs agree (Spearman ρ from %.2f to %.2f between every pair)",
                          rho_pos[1], rho_pos[2])) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5, colour = "#2a78d6"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = MUTED), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
# layer 2: what each model does with the men of the "origin and risk" family
orig_ <- names(fam_of)[fam_of == "origin"]
l2 <- bind_rows(
  D |> filter(country %in% orig_) |> group_by(model) |>
    summarise(`says his origin does not matter` = 100 * mean(defensive_marking),
              `links him to a risk` = 100 * mean(negative_association), .groups = "drop"),
  R |> filter(country %in% orig_) |> group_by(model) |>
    summarise(`refuses to help` = 100 * mean(refusal), .groups = "drop")) |>
  group_by(model) |> summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-model, names_to = "what", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(mod = factor(SHORT[model], levels = rev(SHORT)),
         what = factor(what, levels = c("says his origin does not matter", "links him to a risk", "refuses to help")))
p2 <- ggplot(l2, aes(pct, mod, fill = what)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("says his origin does not matter" = "#eb6834", "links him to a risk" = "#b4232a",
                               "refuses to help" = "#6250d6"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, " %"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "share of answers about Afghan, Nigerian, Maghrebi, Balkan, Indian… men", y = NULL,
       title = "LAYER 2   How each was aligned: what it does with the men it does not compliment",
       subtitle = "each AI its own reflex: defend him, name a risk, refuse to help, or say little") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5, colour = "#d63c2a"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = MUTED), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom", axis.title.x = element_text(size = 7.5))
p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.15))
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** The top layer is shared: whatever the AI, the same men are complimented and the same men are not. The bottom layer is not: for the same men, Granite, Qwen, Gemma 26B and Nemotron mostly say that his origin does not matter, Ministral names a risk, Gemma E2B refuses to help, and Gemma E4B does little of any of it. The first layer looks learnt from shared data; the second, a choice made when each model was aligned.

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

The two layers of bias, measured: compliments by nationality for each model (top, judged answers), and what each model does with the men described by their origin (@fig-words) (bottom; refusals counted on all answers, no judge).
:::

**Two layers, two origins.** Who gets a compliment is shared by seven models from five labs, of every size
tested: such agreement points to what they all learnt from, shared data and the clichés it carries. What a model
does with the other men differs from one model to the next, even between models built on the same base: that
looks like a choice made when each was aligned. The "his origin does not matter" answer is the clearest case. It
presupposes a suspicion the user never expressed, and it is aimed at the same men by four models: a model that
guards against accusations of racism only for some groups reveals that it associates those groups with the
risk. A model neutral on one indicator can be biased on another: a benchmark limited to explicit risks would
have rated the three Gemma models almost perfect, and one limited to a judge would have missed Gemma E2B's refusals.

**The reflex is acquired.** Within the Gemma family, the "his origin does not matter" reflex appears with size
(26B) or with NVIDIA's post-training (Nemotron), and both routes aim it at the same men: it is not a trace of
pre-training data but something a model acquires. A larger model did not become fairer; the bias changed form,
from a refusal the woman can see to a suspicion she may not notice. Across the seven models, size cannot be told
apart from who made the model (the three small ones are all Gemma), so this holds within one family only.

**Confirmed, not found by chance.** The Nigeria · scam signal was declared after the first model (Granite) and
before the other runs; it is found again on Qwen and Ministral, which makes it a confirmatory result rather than
one picked among many. Three readings that share nothing but the answers, the judge, the judge-free classifier
and the refusal count, single out the same men.

**What the pattern follows, and what it does not explain.** The treatment follows the wealth of the man's
country, even within a continent, but the countries also differ by religion, migration history and media
coverage: wealth describes the pattern, not its cause. The religion the AI gives a man goes with the suspicion
without deciding it: it is a marker of the "different culture" box, not a trigger. The most concrete
consequence is for minors: a 15-year-old girl is told to protect herself more or less often depending on the
man's nationality, where the right answer should not depend on it at all.

**What it means in practice.** For those who evaluate models: compare each answer with the same prompt without
the identity (a control), count refusals and unprompted reassurances as bias, not only insults and explicit
risks, and read the answers in the user's language, since the clichés live in the words. For those who use the
models: the advice received depends on who is named, and an answer that sounds balanced can still carry a
suspicion. For those who align them: a reassurance aimed only at some groups is itself a signal of the
association it tries to hide.

**Relation to the RTS report.** I find the "encounter" versus "distrust" contrast described by RTS, attenuated:
these open-weight models rarely tip into outright alarm, and the bias shows only with a repeated design and a control. Ministral is closer
to the report's examples: it is the most alarmist model, and its alarm rises most for Nigeria.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

- **Seven open-weight models, one of them quantised.** Six have 2 to 9 billion parameters (counting the
  effective size of E2B and E4B); Gemma 26B-A4B is a mixture of experts with 4 billion active parameters,
  run in 4-bit AWQ, so its answers are those of the quantised model, which may differ slightly from the
  original. All run on two T4 GPUs; Llama and dense models above 10 billion parameters remain to be done
  (Gemma 4 31B does not fit). One family (Gemma) and one base model / post-training pair (Gemma E4B,
  Nemotron) are too few to generalise what size and post-training do, and across the seven models size cannot
  be told apart from who made the model: the three small ones are all built on Gemma.
- **Refusals are counted by a rule.** The refusal rule (a short answer that opens by declining) was
  checked by reading the answers of every model, but a refusal phrased otherwise would be missed. The
  judge also rates refusals, as neutral answers: they lower Gemma E2B's rates of every indicator without
  being a sign of fairness.
- **The judge is less reliable on some models.** On Ministral, the judge's "defended" verdicts disagree
  with the bench's regular expression (`r pc(by_model(rx_nat, MI, "judge"))` against
  `r pc(by_model(rx_nat, MI, "regex"))`, rank correlation `r num(rx_rho[[MI]], 2)` over nationalities), and
  part of its links to a risk are generic warnings. These two indicators are read with care for
  Ministral; the other models show no such gap.
- **Leftovers in the judge-free analysis.** A few words in the shared vocabulary still point to a place or a
  language rather than to a stereotype (*Canada*, *SAMU*, *gendarmerie*); they are visible in
  the notebook and must not be read as bias. The Reinert classification is simplified (one segment size, no
  double classification as in Iramuteq): its themes are robust enough to read, not to count to the decimal.
- **The judge is a language model.** Qwen3-32B-AWQ can be wrong, and it belongs to the same family as
  Qwen3.5-9B (self-preference cannot be ruled out). The rubric has not been validated against a
  human-annotated sample; reading the quotes shows false positives (for instance a sentence reassuring the
  user about refugee taxi drivers labelled as a "migration" association). The `asks_clarification` field
  remains poorly calibrated for Granite (about 70 % of answers), probably because of offers at the end of
  answers; it is not used in the analysis.
- **Sample size.** About 99 judged answers per nationality and model: gaps of 2 to 3 points are noise,
  and analyses by situation (about 9 verdicts per cell and model) are exploratory.
- **Imperfect masking.** Greetings in the country's language, some city names, or demonyms misspelt by
  the models escape masking and may steer the judge.
- **Wealth is one variable among several.** The link with GDP per capita (@sec-wealth) is measured over
  24 countries; it survives the continent, but the countries also differ by religion and media coverage, so it
  describes the pattern, not its cause.
- **Protocol.** French prompts only, a single gender configuration (a woman alone with a man), and uniform
  generation parameters rather than each vendor's recommended settings.

# Conclusion

I asked seven freely available AI models the same question, 7,425 times each: a woman is alone with a man,
what should she do? Only one word changed from one question to the next, the man's nationality. That word
changes the answer.

- **The same men are complimented everywhere.** All seven AIs, made by five companies, compliment Finns,
  Italians or Japanese, and rarely Afghans or Nigerians.
- **The others are met with suspicion, in different ways.** Some AIs insist that "his origin does not
  matter" (Granite, Qwen, Gemma 26B, Nemotron); one names the risk outright, scams, migration or the
  treatment of women (Ministral, in up to four answers in ten for an Afghan or a Nigerian man); the smallest
  refuses to help (Gemma E2B). Some give him a religion and tell the woman to cover up.
- **Money matters.** The richer his country, the more compliments and the less suspicion, even within a
  continent.
- **Even a 15-year-old girl is protected unequally.** She is told to protect herself less often when the man
  is Japanese or British than when he is Nigerian or Afghan, and no AI protects her every time.
- **Bigger is not fairer.** Within one family of models, the bias changes form with size; it does not go
  away.
- **It shows even without a judge.** With the nationality hidden, a simple program still guesses it from the
  answer six times more often than chance.

These are not the large commercial chatbots of the viral test reported by RTS, but open-weight models that anyone can download, and
the same pattern shows up in all of them. Everything behind this report, prompts, answers, verdicts and
code, is public and can be rerun on free GPUs.

Next steps could be: test Llama and larger models, check the judge and the refusal rule against human readers, and
repeat the study in other languages.
